That’s a very common concern! It’s easy to let the anchor lose its "weight" if the surrounding elements get too busy or too similar to each other. To keep the anchor feeling strong, I suggest a few things: first, make sure the central "anchor" shape has a very distinct, strong visual weight so it’s hard to miss. Second, when placing the "chorus" shapes, make sure they don’t all overlap perfectly—a little bit of "random noise" in the placement will keep it from looking too rigid or boring.

As for your worry about "overcomplicating" the piece: think of the smaller shapes as "supporting" the main idea. If you keep them similar to the anchor but vary their size, you're letting the smaller elements provide *context* rather than *main event*—a perfect way to create that "supporting chorus."

If you want to avoid overwhelming the piece, the key is **contrast**. Ensure the smaller shapes are not too identical to the anchor; let their variance in *scale* or *orientation* give the piece its dynamic flow without losing that sense of "cohesion." Don't try to make every single element identical; let the variance create the rhythm
